title: Cap. XII: Daubuz's arguments do not prove antecedent/immediate imputation
pass_a_gloss: Chapter XII. That antecedent or immediate imputation is not proved by the arguments of Lord Daubuz. For together with Lord Garissoles's book there came forth to him a letter and a send-off poem of Charles Daubuz, minister of the Word in the church at Nerac, in which he warmly praises Garissoles and inveighs against Placeus. He brings forward for the imputation of Adam's sin the same arguments, but in words a little different. He begins from a covenant entered into with Adam, and he assumes that rather than proves it: and he says that we were with Adam; and that as acting and consenting with him and through him we are to be struck with equal punishment. But, I ask you, how were we with Adam, we who then were nobody? For it is prior that we exist than that we exist with another. How did we act with him? For only what exists acts, and indeed a person or a subject: for actions belong to subjects. How did we consent with him and through him? For our consent is an act of our will insofar as we differ from Adam. But if by this consent he means nothing other than the hereditary corruption inborn in us, nothing will be concluded from it beyond mediate imputation, which Placeus proves. He adds as a reason, seeing that by the opinions of the jurisconsults, he who acts through another seems to act through himself. But, I say, that was not to be assumed but proved: that we through Adam did what Adam did. Did he listen to his wife's voice in our place? Were we authors to her that she should sin? Or did he sin as our minister, we as principal causes?
pass_b_english: Chapter XII. That Lord Daubuz's arguments do not prove antecedent or immediate imputation. With Garissoles's book there also appeared a letter and a farewell poem from Charles Daubuz, minister of the Word in the church at Nerac — warm praise for Garissoles, and an attack on Placeus. He urges the same case for imputing Adam's sin, only in slightly different words. He opens from a covenant made with Adam, and he takes that as given rather than proving it. We were with Adam, he says; and as agents and consenters with him and through him we deserve the same penalty. But how, I ask, were we with Adam when we did not yet exist? Existing comes before existing-with-another. How did we act with him? Only what exists acts, and that as a person or subject — for actions belong to subjects. How did we consent with him and through him? Our consent is an act of our own will precisely as we differ from Adam. If by 'consent' he means nothing but the hereditary corruption born in us, he gets only mediate imputation — which Placeus already grants. He adds the lawyers' maxim: whoever acts through another seems to act through himself. That, I say, was not to be assumed but proved: that through Adam we did what Adam did. Did Adam heed his wife in our place? Were we the authors of her sin? Or did he sin as our servant while we were the principal causes?
source_text: CAPUT XII. Imputationem antecedentem seu immediatam non esse probatam argumentis Dom. Daubuz. Nam cum libro D. Garissolii prodit ad eum Epistola & carmen propempticum Caroli Daubuz V.D. in Ecclesia Neracensi Ministri, quibus vehementer eum laudat, & in Placeum invehitur. Affert autem pro imputatione peccati Adamici argumenta eadem, sed verbis paulo diversis. Orditur autem a foedere inito cum Adamo, idque supponit non probat: Aitque nos cum Adamo fuisse; et ut cum eo, ac per eum agentes et consentientes, pari poena plectendos. At, amabo te, quomodo cum Adamo fuimus, qui tunc nulli fuimus? Prius enim est nos esse, quam esse cum alio. Quomodo cum eo egimus? Non enim agit nisi qui est, & quidem persona vel suppositum: actiones enim sunt suppositorum. Quomodo cum eo & per eum consensimus? Est enim consensio nostra voluntatis nostrae, quatenus ab Adamo differimus, actio. Quod si hanc consensionem nihil aliud vult esse quam corruptionem haereditariam nobis ingenitam, ex ea nihil conficietur praeter imputationem mediatam, quam Placeus probat. Addit pro ratione, Quandoquidem ex Iurisconsultorum placitis, qui per alium facit, per se ipsum facere videtur. At, inquam, id erat non supponendum sed probandum, Nos per Adamum id fecisse, quod fecit Adamus. Auscultavitne voci uxoris suae loco nostro? nosne illi fuimus autores ut peccaret? aut peccavitne ut minister noster, nos ut causae principales?
